changes.current_line: Every payout reconciles automatically to its transactions and your ERP.
changes.change: For finance buyers, lead the first call with this, in their words: "Know where your money is. Every deposit matched to its transactions and your ERP, so month-end isn't a week of archaeology." Use it ahead of M1 and M2 for distributors and other non-developer, non-global buyers.
changes.why: Ines stopped the demo on payout reconciliation after the opening deck got silence, and her own phrases ("where my money is", "a week of archaeology") describe the problem more sharply than our line does.

changes.current_line: Proven ROI, backed by an independent economic impact study.
changes.change: Send us one month of your statements and we'll show you your own hours and dollars: what matching deposits by hand costs you at your rates, and what you'd get back. Use for finance decision-makers evaluating a switch from a bank-bundled processor.
changes.why: Ines moved from doubt to "that's my number, not yours" when the case was built from her own statements, and nothing in the interview suggests the independent study mattered.

changes.current_line: Financial infrastructure to grow globally, in every currency.
changes.change: Do not open with this on first calls to finance leaders at regional, non-developer businesses (e.g., a distributor with a small IT team and no build plans). Keep it for global or developer-led buyers. Retire "infrastructure" from CFO-facing copy; use "deposits" and "month-end" instead.
changes.why: The standard opener got silence from a regional distributor, and nobody on the buyer side ever said "infrastructure" or even "payments"; they said "the deposits" and "the processor".

changes.current_line: Support plans with tiered response times, up to 24/7 coverage.
changes.change: For buyers leaving a bank-bundled incumbent: "You get a named contact who knows your business and answers your actual problem, not a rate quote." Name the people, not the tiers.
changes.why: The incumbent answered a business-problem call with "we can take a look at your rates", and after that Ines asked whether she'd get a named contact, which suggests service continuity mattered to her.
